sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a Spring AI application concept and how it fits into an end-to-end application. The goal is to understand the reason for the abstraction, not merely memorize an API name.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Spring AI is a Spring ecosystem project designed to make it easier for Java and
Spring developers to build applications that use AI models.

The central problem is not simply "how do I call an LLM?"

A real application often needs to connect:

```text
User
  |
  v
Spring application
  |
  +---- AI model
  |
  +---- company database
  |
  +---- APIs
  |
  +---- documents
  |
  +---- vector database
  |
  +---- tools and business services
```
Spring AI provides abstractions so that application code does not have to be
completely tied to one AI provider.

For example, an application can use a ChatModel abstraction instead of directly
building every integration around one vendor SDK.

**Why This Matters**

Without an abstraction layer, an application can become tightly coupled to:

- Provider-specific request classes
- Provider-specific response classes
- Provider-specific configuration
- Provider-specific streaming APIs
- Provider-specific tool-calling mechanisms
Spring AI attempts to put a common Spring-friendly API in front of these
capabilities.

Spring AI describes the project's central integration problem as:

Connecting enterprise data and APIs with AI models.

**Important Mindset**

Spring AI is not itself an AI model.

It is an application framework and abstraction layer that helps Spring developers
work with AI models and AI application patterns.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Imagine a Spring Boot service using **What Spring AI is** to support an internal developer assistant. The application receives a request, applies the topic's mechanism, validates the result, and exposes only the information and capabilities the caller is authorized to use.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **What Spring AI is** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **What Spring AI is** as one component in a larger request flow. Understand what enters it, what state it depends on, what it returns, and which guarantees the application can actually rely on.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is What Spring AI is, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **What Spring AI is** include: Memorizing method names without understanding the request flow; using the feature where a simpler approach is enough; ignoring provider-specific behavior; and skipping validation and failure handling.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **What Spring AI is** when it directly supports the application's access pattern or reliability requirement. Avoid adding the abstraction solely because it is available; choose the simplest design that meets the product's constraints.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In a production Spring AI service, **What Spring AI is** should have an explicit owner, configuration boundary, timeout/failure policy, observability signal, and security review. Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. Keep secrets outside source control and avoid exposing internal prompts, credentials, or private customer data through logs or model context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic matters because an AI demo and a production service have different requirements. Reliability, security, observability, cost, latency, capacity, and failure behavior must be designed deliberately.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Spring AI follows several important design ideas.

**1. Portability**

The same conceptual API can be used with multiple model providers.

Example:

```text
ChatClient
    |
    v
ChatModel abstraction
    |
    +---- OpenAI
    +---- Anthropic
    +---- Google
    +---- Mistral
    +---- Ollama
    +---- Bedrock
    +---- other providers
```
The exact model capabilities can differ, but the application can keep a
provider-neutral programming model for common operations.

**2. Composability**

Spring AI features can be combined.

A single application can use:

```java
ChatClient
    +
Chat memory
    +
RAG
    +
Tool calling
    +
Observability
```

**3. Spring Boot Integration**

Configuration and dependency management follow familiar Spring Boot patterns.

**4. Model-Specific Escape Hatches**

Portability does not mean every provider-specific feature disappears.

When an application needs provider-specific functionality, Spring AI allows
developers to access model-specific options and capabilities.

sections.content: Consider a production AI endpoint receiving thousands of requests per hour. For **Spring AI architecture and design philosophy**, the team needs measurable latency, token usage, error rates, safe logging, bounded retries, explicit timeouts, and a recovery or fallback strategy rather than relying on a happy-path demo.

sections.content: Common pitfalls for **Spring AI architecture and design philosophy** include: Logging sensitive prompts or responses; using unbounded retries; omitting timeouts; measuring only success rate; ignoring token cost; and designing no fallback or degraded mode for provider failures.

sections.title: When to use / avoid

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Spring AI works with several categories of AI models.

**Chat Models**

Input usually consists of messages or prompts.

Output is generated conversational content.

Typical use:

Question -> Chat model -> Answer

**Embedding Models**

Input is converted into numerical vectors.

Typical use:

Document -> embedding vector -> vector database

**Image Models**

Generate images from prompts.

Typical use:

Text description -> image model -> generated image

**Transcription Models**

Convert audio to text.

Typical use:

Audio -> speech-to-text model -> text

**Text-To-Speech Models**

Convert text to spoken audio.

Typical use:

Text -> TTS model -> audio

**Moderation Models**

Can be used to assess generated or submitted content according to a model's
moderation capabilities.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic sits at the Spring AI integration layer: dependencies, configuration, provider implementations, or deployment choices. The goal is predictable configuration and a clear boundary between portable application code and provider-specific behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A major Spring AI idea is to separate:

Application-level AI logic
from
Provider-specific implementation.
Suppose an application has:

```java
String answer = chatClient.prompt()
    .user("Explain dependency injection")
    .call()
    .content();
```
The application is expressing what it wants to do.

The actual model provider can be configured separately.

This makes it easier to:

- switch models
- compare providers
- use different models for different tasks
- implement fallback strategies
- test against local models
- reduce vendor lock-in

**Portability Has Limits**

Different models support different capabilities.

For example:

- Model A -> text only
- Model B -> text + image
- Model C -> text + image + audio
- Model D -> local execution
Therefore, portable application code should rely on capabilities common to the
chosen models, while provider-specific features should be isolated.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Imagine the same Spring Boot service running in development against a local model and in production against a hosted provider. For **Provider portability**, keep provider credentials and provider-specific options outside business logic, verify supported capabilities, and test the effective configuration in each environment.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Provider portability** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Provider portability** as configuration and integration plumbing. Business logic should express the application's intent while environment-specific credentials, endpoints, model names, and provider options remain configurable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is Provider portability, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **Provider portability** include: Copying configuration blindly between environments; committing credentials; mixing incompatible dependency versions; assuming every provider exposes identical capabilities; and failing to verify the actual model selected at runtime.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **Provider portability** to make integrations reproducible and configurable. Avoid coupling business logic directly to environment-specific credentials or provider details when a portable boundary is sufficient.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Spring AI provides a Bill of Materials (BOM).

The purpose of a BOM is to keep compatible versions of Spring AI modules aligned.

Conceptually:

```text
spring-ai-bom
     |
     +---- model module
     +---- vector store module
     +---- supporting modules
```
Using the BOM avoids manually assigning unrelated versions to every Spring AI
dependency.

For production projects, version management should be deliberate and consistent.

Example:

Explain dependency injection.
The model combines these messages according to the provider's API semantics.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Prompt templates allow dynamic values to be inserted into reusable instructions.

Example:

"Explain {topic} for a {experienceLevel} developer."
Runtime values:

- topic = "Spring Security"
- experienceLevel = "beginner"
Rendered prompt:

Explain Spring Security for a beginner developer.
Spring AI uses StringTemplate for prompt template functionality.

**Why Templates Help**

Without templates, applications often create strings manually.

With templates:

- fixed instruction
- +
- runtime variables
- =
- consistent prompt
This improves maintainability and makes prompts easier to reuse.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
AI models process tokens rather than raw human words.

A token can represent part of a word, a complete word, punctuation, or another
piece of text depending on the tokenizer.

**Token Usage Matters For Three Reasons**

1. Cost

Many hosted models charge according to input/output token usage.

2. Context limits

A model can process only a bounded amount of context per request.

3. Performance

Very large prompts can increase latency and processing cost.

Example:

- User question
- +
- system instructions
- +
- chat history
- +
- retrieved documents
- +
- tool results
- =
- total context
If everything is included blindly, the application can exceed the model's
context window.

This is one reason RAG retrieval and document chunking are important.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An embedding is a numerical representation of information.

Example:

"Spring Boot is a Java framework."
might be transformed conceptually into:

[0.12, -0.48, 0.91,  ]
The vector itself is not meant to be read by humans.

Its purpose is to represent semantic characteristics in a mathematical space.

SIMILARITY

Suppose:

- Document A = "Spring Boot REST API"
- Query      = "How do I create REST endpoints?"
Their embeddings may be relatively close because their meanings are related.

This enables semantic search.

**Embedding Dimension**

The number of values in the vector is its dimensionality.

Example:

```text
[0.1, 0.4, -0.2, ]
 <---- many dimensions ---->
```
The dimensionality must be compatible with the vector-store configuration.

IMPORTANT

An embedding model is not the same as a chat model.

Chat model:

prompt -> generated response
Embedding model:

text/document -> vector

topics.title: Structured output
topics.description: AI models commonly return text. But applications often need an actual Java object.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
AI models commonly return text.

But applications often need an actual Java object.

Example desired result:

```java
class Product {
    String name;
    double price;
}
```
A model might return:

- {
- "name": "Laptop",
- "price": 999.0
- }

That response is initially text.

The application still needs to convert it into:

Product
Spring AI provides structured output converters for this purpose.

Important implementations include:

```java
BeanOutputConverter
MapOutputConverter
ListOutputConverter
```

**Structured Output Is Not Magic**

A model can still generate malformed or unexpected output.

Therefore applications should consider:

- schema constraints
- validation
- conversion failures
- retries
- model support
- error handling

topics.description: RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. Basic flow: The model generates the answer using retrieved context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation.

Basic flow:

```text
Documents
   |
   v
Read
   |
   v
Split
   |
   v
Embed
   |
   v
Vector Store
   |
   |  similarity search
   v
Relevant documents
   |
   v
Prompt + context
   |
   v
Chat Model
   |
   v
Answer
```
The model generates the answer using retrieved context.

**Why Rag Works**

Instead of giving the model an entire document collection, retrieve the pieces
that are most relevant to the user's question.

topics.title: Tool calling
topics.description: Tool calling allows an AI model to request application-defined operations. Examples: - getWeather(city) - findCustomer(id) - getAccountBalance(id) -

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Tool calling allows an AI model to request application-defined operations.

Examples:

- getWeather(city)
- findCustomer(id)
- getAccountBalance(id)
- searchProducts(query)
- sendEmail(to, body)
The model does not directly receive unrestricted access to the underlying API.

The application owns tool execution.

Typical flow:

```text
User request
   |
   v
ChatClient
   |
   v
AI model
   |
   | "I need tool X with arguments Y"
   v
Spring AI tool mechanism
   |
   v
Application function
   |
   v
Tool result
   |
   v
AI model
   |
   v
Final response
```
This pattern is a foundation for agentic applications.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **Tool calling**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
PROMPT

Represents the model input.

It contains messages and optional chat options.

MESSAGE

Represents one unit of conversational input/output.

CHATOPTIONS

Contains portable generation parameters such as:

- model
- temperature
- max tokens
- top-p
- top-k
- stop sequences
- frequency penalty
- presence penalty
Not every provider necessarily implements every option identically.

CHATRESPONSE

Represents the standardized model response.

It can contain one or more generations and metadata.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The EmbeddingModel abstraction provides a portable interface for turning text
or document content into vectors.

Important operations conceptually include:

- embed(String)
- embed(Document)
- embedForResponse()
- dimensions()
The API wraps embedding input and output in:

- EmbeddingRequest
- EmbeddingResponse
- Embedding
The result is typically a floating-point vector.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A documentation assistant illustrates **Embedding Model API**: a user asks about an internal API, the application prepares or retrieves the relevant document content, and only the selected context is passed to the model. The implementation should record document identity and retrieval metadata so the answer can be traced back to its source.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Embedding Model API** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Embedding Model API** as a pipeline with explicit boundaries: source -> transformation -> retrieval/selection -> context -> generation -> evaluation. A weakness in an earlier stage can look like a model problem later, so troubleshoot the stages separately.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic deals with AI inputs or outputs beyond plain text. The important engineering question is not only how to pass media, but whether the selected model supports the modality, how media is represented, and how failures and size limits are handled.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The Image Model API provides a portable interface for image generation.

Important concepts:

- ImageModel
- ImagePrompt
- ImageResponse
- ImageGeneration
- Image metadata

ImageResponse can contain multiple generated images.

The abstraction allows applications to work with different image model
implementations using a common API.

Available implementations in the Spring AI reference include:

- OpenAI Image Generation
- Stability AI Image Generation
- Google GenAI Image Generation

sections.content: A product-support assistant receives a user question plus an image of a device. - Message:

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Chat memory stores conversation history.

Without memory:

- User: My name is Alex.
- Assistant: Nice to meet you.
- User: What is my name?
The model may not know the previous message unless history is supplied.

With memory:

```text
conversation id
    |
    v
stored messages
    |
    v
current request
    |
    v
model
```
Spring AI provides ChatMemory abstractions.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
ChatClient can combine advisors for memory and RAG.

Conceptual example:

```text
ChatClient
   |
   +---- MessageChatMemoryAdvisor
   |
   +---- QuestionAnswerAdvisor
   |
   +---- ChatModel
```
The memory advisor can supply conversation context.

The RAG advisor can retrieve relevant documents.

The model then receives a richer prompt.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A documentation assistant illustrates **RAG through ChatClient**: a user asks about an internal API, the application prepares or retrieves the relevant document content, and only the selected context is passed to the model. The implementation should record document identity and retrieval metadata so the answer can be traced back to its source.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **RAG through ChatClient** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **RAG through ChatClient** as a pipeline with explicit boundaries: source -> transformation -> retrieval/selection -> context -> generation -> evaluation. A weakness in an earlier stage can look like a model problem later, so troubleshoot the stages separately.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Advisors are reusable components that can inspect and modify AI requests and
responses.

They are useful for implementing recurring AI application patterns.

Examples:

- memory
- RAG
- logging
- tool calling
- prompt transformation
- reasoning strategies
Instead of putting all logic inside a controller, advisors let the behavior
be composed around the model interaction.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
ToolCallingAdvisor manages the tool-calling loop in the ChatClient architecture.

The high-level flow is:

```text
request
  |
  v
model
  |
  | tool call?
  v
ToolCallingManager
  |
  v
ToolCallback
  |
  v
tool result
  |
  v
model
  |
  v
final response
```

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **ToolCallingAdvisor**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **ToolCallingAdvisor** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **ToolCallingAdvisor** as a capability boundary, not as permission for the model to run arbitrary code. The model proposes an action; application code decides whether that action is valid and allowed.

sections.title: Interview focus

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Spring AI 2.x makes the tool-calling loop a first-class component of the
ChatClient advisor chain.

High-level flow:

```java
1. Define tools.
2. Register tools with ChatClient.
3. Send request.
4. Model decides whether to call a tool.
5. ToolCallingManager executes the selected callback.
6. Tool result is added to the conversation.
7. Model receives the result.
8. Loop continues until no more tool calls are requested.
```

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic matters because an AI demo and a production service have different requirements. Reliability, security, observability, cost, latency, capacity, and failure behavior must be designed deliberately.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A critical security principle:

The model does not receive unrestricted access to your application APIs.

The application owns the execution mechanism.

Still, the application must validate:

- tool arguments
- authorization
- tenant boundaries
- user permissions
- destructive actions
- external side effects
Never assume that because a model requested a tool, the action is automatically
authorized.

For **Security boundaries**, the team needs measurable latency, token usage, error rates, safe logging, bounded retries, explicit timeouts, and a recovery or fallback strategy rather than relying on a happy-path demo.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A vector database stores vector representations and supports similarity search.

Traditional database query:

WHERE name = 'Spring'
Vector search:

Find vectors most similar to the query vector.
This is useful when exact keyword matching is insufficient.

The implementation should record document identity and retrieval metadata so the answer can be traced back to its source.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A Document is the core unit moving through the ETL pipeline.

It can contain:

- text
- metadata
- media

Metadata is especially important because retrieval often needs filters.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A documentation assistant illustrates **Document**: a user asks about an internal API, the application prepares or retrieves the relevant document content, and only the selected context is passed to the model. The implementation should record document identity and retrieval metadata so the answer can be traced back to its source.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Document** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Document** as a pipeline with explicit boundaries: source -> transformation -> retrieval/selection -> context -> generation -> evaluation. A weakness in an earlier stage can look like a model problem later, so troubleshoot the stages separately.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is Document, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **Document** include: Using retrieval as a guarantee of factuality; retrieving too many chunks; ignoring metadata and source identity; mixing incompatible embedding dimensions; and failing to measure retrieval quality separately from generation quality.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **Document** when application answers depend on external or changing information and the mechanism in this topic improves retrieval or grounding. Avoid it when a simpler direct lookup or deterministic application query answers the question more reliably.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In a production Spring AI service, **Document** should have an explicit owner, configuration boundary, timeout/failure policy, observability signal, and security review. Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. modules.description: Learn MCP through clear explanations, practical examples, and application-focused guidance.

topics.title: What MCP is
topics.description: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It standardizes how AI applications interact with external tools and resources.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.

It standardizes how AI applications interact with external tools and resources.

Think of MCP as a protocol boundary between:

```text
AI application
    |
    v
standardized MCP interface
    |
    +---- tools
    +---- resources
    +---- prompts
    |
    v
external system
```
Spring AI supports both consuming MCP servers and exposing Spring services
through MCP.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **What MCP is**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **What MCP is** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **What MCP is** as a capability boundary, not as permission for the model to run arbitrary code. The model proposes an action; application code decides whether that action is valid and allowed.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is What MCP is, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **What MCP is** include: Treating model-generated arguments as trusted input; exposing destructive operations without authorization; giving tools excessive scope; leaking secrets through tool results; and assuming tool calling is identical across models.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **What MCP is** when the model needs a controlled application capability. Avoid exposing a tool when the same result can be computed deterministically in application code, or when the operation is too dangerous to delegate without a stronger approval boundary.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In a production Spring AI service, **What MCP is** should have an explicit owner, configuration boundary, timeout/failure policy, observability signal, and security review. Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. Keep secrets outside source control and avoid exposing internal prompts, credentials, or private customer data through logs or model context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
ChatClient observations can measure invocation time and propagate tracing
information.

Additional contextual information can include:

- streaming status
- advisors
- conversation ID
- tool names

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For **ChatClient observations**, imagine a Spring Boot endpoint that receives a user request, constructs the appropriate prompt or model input, invokes the selected model, and validates the returned result before exposing it to downstream business logic. The important design choice is to make model capabilities and failure handling explicit.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **ChatClient observations** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **ChatClient observations** as a boundary between application intent and model execution. Inputs are assembled, provider/model behavior occurs behind the abstraction, and the application must still validate the returned result.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is ChatClient observations, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **ChatClient observations** include: Hard-coding provider-specific assumptions into business logic; ignoring timeouts and errors; trusting generated output without validation; and tuning parameters without measuring quality, latency, and cost.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **ChatClient observations** when its model-facing abstraction solves a real application requirement. Avoid overengineering the model layer when a deterministic Java service can solve the requirement more reliably.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In a production Spring AI service, **ChatClient observations** should have an explicit owner, configuration boundary, timeout/failure policy, observability signal, and security review. Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. Keep secrets outside source control and avoid exposing internal prompts, credentials, or private customer data through logs or model context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic focuses on state around an AI interaction. A useful design separates the user's conversation identity, stored history, context selection, prompt construction, and model invocation instead of treating memory as an unlimited transcript.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Advisor observations track execution of advisors.

This is useful for understanding:

- advisor latency
- chain order
- slow retrieval
- slow custom logic

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Consider a support chat where conversation `case-4812` contains earlier messages. For **Advisor observations**, the application should deliberately decide which history is loaded, how much is retained, and whether sensitive messages are eligible for persistence before sending context to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Advisor observations** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Advisor observations** as controlled context management. Conversation identity tells you whose state is involved, storage determines what survives, and context selection determines what the model actually sees.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is Advisor observations, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **Advisor observations** include: Treating memory as unlimited; sending sensitive history by default; mixing users or conversation IDs; assuming stored history is automatically relevant; and allowing context growth to drive cost and latency without bounds.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **Advisor observations** when continuity across requests is part of the product requirement. Avoid retaining more history than the model needs; summarize, window, or retrieve state when that produces a smaller and safer context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Tool observations can record:

- tool name
- tool type
- tool call ID
- execution timing
Tool arguments/results are not exported by default because they may contain
sensitive information.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **Tool observations**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Tool observations** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Tool observations** as a capability boundary, not as permission for the model to run arbitrary code. The model proposes an action; application code decides whether that action is valid and allowed.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is Tool observations, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **Tool observations** include: Treating model-generated arguments as trusted input; exposing destructive operations without authorization; giving tools excessive scope; leaking secrets through tool results; and assuming tool calling is identical across models.

sections.title: When to use / avoid

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic is about how Spring AI moves information through a retrieval-oriented workflow. The key is to separate source data, retrieval, context construction, and generation so each stage can be measured and changed independently.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Embedding operations can expose model and token usage observations.

the Spring AI reference notes provider-specific observability support for
certain embedding implementations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A documentation assistant illustrates **Embedding observations**: a user asks about an internal API, the application prepares or retrieves the relevant document content, and only the selected context is passed to the model. The implementation should record document identity and retrieval metadata so the answer can be traced back to its source.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Embedding observations** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Embedding observations** as a pipeline with explicit boundaries: source -> transformation -> retrieval/selection -> context -> generation -> evaluation. A weakness in an earlier stage can look like a model problem later, so troubleshoot the stages separately.

sections.title: Interview focus

Image model operations can also participate in observability.

Controller

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic sits at the Spring AI integration layer: dependencies, configuration, provider implementations, or deployment choices. The goal is predictable configuration and a clear boundary between portable application code and provider-specific behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
OpenAI integration supports chat models and other AI capabilities.

the Spring AI reference includes support for:

- text
- vision
- audio
- tool calling
- streaming
- structured output capabilities

OpenAI image generation is also supported.

Credentials should be provided securely through configuration.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Imagine the same Spring Boot service running in development against a local model and in production against a hosted provider. For **OpenAI**, keep provider credentials and provider-specific options outside business logic, verify supported capabilities, and test the effective configuration in each environment.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **OpenAI** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **OpenAI** as configuration and integration plumbing. Business logic should express the application's intent while environment-specific credentials, endpoints, model names, and provider options remain configurable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is OpenAI, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls for **OpenAI** include: Copying configuration blindly between environments; committing credentials; mixing incompatible dependency versions; assuming every provider exposes identical capabilities; and failing to verify the actual model selected at runtime.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use **OpenAI** to make integrations reproducible and configurable. Avoid coupling business logic directly to environment-specific credentials or provider details when a portable boundary is sufficient.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In a production Spring AI service, **OpenAI** should have an explicit owner, configuration boundary, timeout/failure policy, observability signal, and security review. Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. Keep secrets outside source control and avoid exposing internal prompts, credentials, or private customer data through logs or model context.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Local deployment is useful when:

- privacy is important
- internet access is restricted
- predictable infrastructure is required
- experimentation is needed
Ollama is one of the integrations listed for local deployment.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For **Local model deployment**, imagine a Spring Boot endpoint that receives a user request, constructs the appropriate prompt or model input, invokes the selected model, and validates the returned result before exposing it to downstream business logic. The important design choice is to make model capabilities and failure handling explicit.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Local model deployment** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **Local model deployment** as a boundary between application intent and model execution. Inputs are assembled, provider/model behavior occurs behind the abstraction, and the application must still validate the returned result.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is Local model deployment, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. Avoid claiming that Spring AI or a model guarantees behavior that actually depends on the selected provider, model, configuration, or application code.

sections.title: Common pitfalls

sections.title: When to use / avoid

sections.title: Production scenario

Test normal traffic as well as malformed input, provider errors, slow responses, retries, and unexpected model output. sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Example:

- User:
- "What is the weather in Delhi?"
- Model:
- calls getWeather("Delhi")
- Tool:
- returns weather
- Model:
- creates final answer
The tool is controlled by the application.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **Tool-enabled assistant**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Tool-enabled assistant** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:

ingestion application

vector database

query application

retrieval
    |

ChatClient
    |
    v
model

For large systems, ingestion and query processing may be separate services.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A documentation assistant illustrates **RAG application**: a user asks about an internal API, the application prepares or retrieves the relevant document content, and only the selected context is passed to the model. sections.title: Practical use

sections.title: Deep mental model

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic concerns controlled interaction between a model and application-owned capabilities. The model can request an operation, but the application remains responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, executing the operation, and returning a safe result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An application can connect to MCP servers and make their tools available to
the AI model.

Example:

```text
Spring AI application
      |
      v
MCP client
      |
      v
Weather MCP server
      |
      v
weather API
```

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose an assistant must answer, "What is the status of order 4812?" For **MCP-enabled application**, the model can request an application-owned operation with the order identifier. The server validates the identifier, authorization, and tool arguments before executing the operation, then returns a bounded result to the model.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **MCP-enabled application** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of **MCP-enabled application** as a capability boundary, not as permission for the model to run arbitrary code. The model proposes an action; application code decides whether that action is valid and allowed.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interviewer may ask: **What is MCP-enabled application, why would you use it, and what trade-off does it introduce?** A strong answer should define the concept, show a small Spring AI example, explain where it sits in the request flow, mention one failure mode, and compare it with the closest alternative. sections.title: Common pitfalls

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic explains a model-facing Spring AI concept. The central mental model is an application request becoming a typed or structured model interaction, followed by a response that must be interpreted according to the model's capabilities and the application's contract.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Use ChatClient when:

- fluent application development is desired
- advisors are needed
- tools are needed
- memory is needed
- application code should be concise
Use ChatModel directly when:

- lower-level control is needed
- implementing custom infrastructure
- integrating with specialized model logic
For most normal Spring application code, ChatClient is the more convenient
high-level abstraction.

Start with the smallest working configuration, make provider and model assumptions explicit, then add validation, error handling, and observability before treating the feature as production-ready.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Q: What is Spring AI?

A:
Spring AI is a Spring ecosystem project that provides abstractions and
integrations for building AI applications with models, vector stores, tools,
RAG, memory, observability and related capabilities.

Q: What is ChatClient?

A:
A fluent higher-level API for interacting with chat models.

Q: ChatClient vs ChatModel?

A:
ChatModel is a lower-level model abstraction. ChatClient provides a more
convenient application-level fluent API and integrates naturally with advisors,
tools and memory.

Q: What is an embedding?

A:
A numerical vector representation used to capture semantic relationships.

Q: Why is a vector database used in RAG?

A:
It allows similarity-based retrieval of relevant document chunks.

Q: What is RAG?

A:
Retrieval Augmented Generation retrieves relevant external information and
adds it to the model context before generation.

Q: What is tool calling?

A:
A mechanism where a model requests application-defined functions and the
application executes them and returns the results.

Q: Does the model directly execute a Java method?

A:
No. The application owns tool execution. The model requests a tool call and
the application executes the corresponding tool.

Q: What is an Advisor?

A:
A reusable component that can inspect, transform or augment AI requests and
responses.

Q: What is MCP?

A:
A standardized protocol for connecting AI applications with external tools,
resources and prompts.

Q: Why is chunking important in RAG?

A:
Because retrieval operates on stored document pieces. Poor chunks can lose
meaning or return irrelevant context.

sections.content:

- lower-level

- more control
ChatClient:
- fluent API
- higher-level application abstraction
- easy advisor/tool/memory integration
CHAT MODEL vs EMBEDDING MODEL

Chat:
generates responses
Embedding:
generates vectors
RAG vs FINE-TUNING

RAG:
retrieves external/current information at request time
Fine-tuning:
changes model behavior/weights through additional training
VECTOR DATABASE vs RELATIONAL DATABASE

Vector database:
similarity-oriented retrieval
Relational database:
structured transactional/query-oriented storage
TOOL CALLING vs RAG

RAG:
retrieves information
Tool calling:
executes application operations or retrieves dynamic data
MEMORY vs RAG

Memory:
preserves conversation context
RAG:
retrieves external knowledge
MCP vs TOOL CALLBACK

ToolCallback:
Spring AI's application-level tool execution abstraction
MCP:
- standardized protocol for exposing/consuming tools and resources across
- application boundaries

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: This topic matters because an AI demo and a production service have different requirements. Reliability, security, observability, cost, latency, capacity, and failure behavior must be designed deliberately.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
MODEL

- [ ] Correct model selected
- [ ] Capability compatibility verified
- [ ] Timeout configured
- [ ] Retry strategy considered
- [ ] Cost monitored
SECURITY

```java
[ ] API keys stored securely
[ ] Tool authorization implemented
[ ] Sensitive prompts protected
[ ] Prompt logs reviewed
[ ] MCP endpoints secured
[ ] Tenant isolation enforced
```
RAG

- [ ] Document sources identified
- [ ] Chunking strategy tested
- [ ] Metadata defined
- [ ] Embedding model selected
- [ ] Vector store selected
- [ ] Retrieval quality measured
- [ ] Stale documents handled
TOOLS

```java
[ ] Descriptions are clear
[ ] Arguments validated
[ ] Authorization checked
[ ] Dangerous actions protected
[ ] Tool latency measured
```
OBSERVABILITY

- [ ] Metrics enabled
- [ ] Tracing enabled
- [ ] Token usage monitored
- [ ] Errors monitored
- [ ] Model latency monitored
- [ ] Tool execution monitored
OUTPUT

- [ ] Structured output validated
- [ ] Conversion errors handled
- [ ] Model failures handled
- [ ] Fallback behavior defined

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Consider a production AI endpoint receiving thousands of requests per hour. For **Production checklist**, the team needs measurable latency, token usage, error rates, safe logging, bounded retries, explicit timeouts, and a recovery or fallback strategy rather than relying on a happy-path demo.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: In a real Spring AI project, **Production checklist** should be introduced only after the requirement and access pattern are clear. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
**Spring Ai Basics**

- [ ] What is Spring AI?
- [ ] Why use abstractions?
- [ ] What is provider portability?
- [ ] What does Spring Boot auto-configuration do?

**Ai Concepts**

- [ ] Model
- [ ] Prompt
- [ ] Message
- [ ] Token
- [ ] Context window
- [ ] Embedding
- [ ] Structured output
- [ ] RAG

**Core Apis**

```java
[ ] ChatModel
[ ] StreamingChatModel
[ ] ChatClient
[ ] EmbeddingModel
[ ] ImageModel
[ ] Audio models
[ ] VectorStore
```
CHATCLIENT

- [ ] prompt()
- [ ] user()
- [ ] system()
- [ ] call()
- [ ] stream()
- [ ] content()
- [ ] advisors()
- [ ] tools()
- [ ] defaultTools()
- [ ] memory

ADVISORS

- [ ] Advisor chain
- [ ] Ordering
- [ ] Memory advisor
- [ ] QuestionAnswerAdvisor
- [ ] RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor
- [ ] ReReadingAdvisor
- [ ] ToolCallingAdvisor
- [ ] Custom advisor

RAG

```java
[ ] Document
[ ] Reader
[ ] Transformer
[ ] Writer
[ ] Chunking
[ ] Embedding
[ ] VectorStore
[ ] Similarity search
[ ] Metadata filter
[ ] Context assembly
```
TOOLS

```java
[ ] @Tool
[ ] @ToolParam
[ ] MethodToolCallback
[ ] FunctionToolCallback
[ ] ToolCallback
[ ] ToolCallingAdvisor
[ ] Security validation
```
MCP

- [ ] Client
- [ ] Server
- [ ] Tools
- [ ] Resources
- [ ] Prompts
- [ ] STDIO
- [ ] SSE
- [ ] Streamable HTTP
- [ ] Annotations
- [ ] Boot starters
- [ ] Security

OBSERVABILITY

- [ ] Metrics
- [ ] Tracing
- [ ] Token usage
- [ ] Tool observations
- [ ] Prompt logging
- [ ] Sensitive data
PRODUCTION

- [ ] Security
- [ ] Cost
- [ ] Latency
- [ ] Reliability
- [ ] Retrieval quality
- [ ] Model capability
- [ ] Monitoring
- [ ] Evaluation

**Final Mental Model**

The easiest way to understand Spring AI is to see it as a collection of layers.

**Layer 1 — Model**

- Chat
- Embedding
- Image
- Audio

**Layer 2 — Application Api**

```java
ChatClient
Prompt
Message
Options
Response
```

**Layer 3 — Context**

```java
Memory
RAG
VectorStore
Advisors
```

**Layer 4 — Actions**

- Tools
- Tool calling
- MCP

**Layer 5 — Data Engineering**

- DocumentReader
- DocumentTransformer
- DocumentWriter
- ETL
- Chunking
- Embeddings
- Vector storage

**Layer 6 — Operations**

- Observability
- Metrics
- Tracing
- Evaluation
- Security

The complete picture is:

```text
USER
  |
  v
SPRING BOOT APPLICATION
  |
  v
CHATCLIENT
  |
  +-------------------+
  |                   |
  v                   v
ADVISORS            TOOLS
  |                   |
  +----+--------------+
       |
       v
    CONTEXT
    /     \\
 MEMORY    RAG
            |
            v
       VECTOR STORE
            |
            v
      RETRIEVED DATA
            |
            v
       CHAT MODEL
            |
            v
         ANSWER
```
And when the model needs to perform an action:

```text
CHAT MODEL
    |
    v
TOOL CALL
    |
    v
APPLICATION
    |
    v
EXTERNAL API / DATABASE / SERVICE
    |
    v
TOOL RESULT
    |
    v
CHAT MODEL
    |
    v
FINAL ANSWER
```
The central engineering principle is:

- The model generates intelligence,
- the application controls the system,
- retrieval supplies knowledge,
- tools provide actions,
- memory supplies conversation context,
- and observability/evaluation make the system measurable and safer.
